title: Grace at the table
tomorrow: can a sink full of dishes be a prayer?

cards: Plates down, steam rising, somebody already reaching for the rolls. Then somebody says, wait. At some Christian tables that's when grace comes: before the first bite.
But the Torah's own command about blessing God for food sits at the other end of the meal.
In the JPS translation, a Jewish one: “And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee.” Eat first. Be satisfied.

teach.b: So why pause over food at all? The Gospels show Jesus doing it.
Before feeding the crowd, he “took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples.”
At Emmaus, at a simple supper, he takes bread and blesses it, and that's when the two disciples know him.

teach.h: PAUL GAVE THANKS IN A STORM.
teach.b: Paul does it on a ship in a storm, everyone frightened and hungry: he “took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all.”
Christian tables keep it in different forms: Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, in some Catholic homes; Come, Lord Jesus, be our guest, in some Lutheran ones; a plain thank you; or silence.
The answer underneath is the same: the pause turns food back into a gift. Now the neighbor.
That verse from Deuteronomy is where Jewish tradition roots its grace after meals, the Birkat Hamazon, and the Mishnah also gives short blessings to say before eating, like the one over bread.

teach.h: ONE GIFT, THANKED IN TWO WAYS.
teach.b: Jews and Christians share this: food is a gift, and the giver is thanked. Jesus, a Jew, blessed bread before he broke it. The honest difference is in the form.
Jewish law sets the Torah's blessing after the meal, in its own words and order; the Christian graces here come before the first bite, and some end in Jesus' name.

how: Christian households say grace in different ways: a set prayer such as Bless us, O Lord, a sung blessing, a few plain words of thanks or a moment of silence.

games.q: what does “grace at the table” mean?
o: a polite rule about waiting for the host
a short thanks to God said over a meal
free food that a church gives to its guests

games.q: thanks at the table — tap the pairs.
p: looking up to heaven, he blessed
gave thanks in presence of them all

s: the Torah's command to bless God for food comes after eating
eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God.
grace is only for big family meals
Paul gave thanks over bread on a ship in a storm.
Jews and Christians bless God for food in exactly the same way
both thank God for food; the timing, words and order differ.

games.q: a friend says grace is pointless: "i paid for the food." what does today's answer offer him?
o: grace is mostly good manners for when guests are over.
the pause turns food back into a gift, whoever paid for it.
grace is really meant for big holiday dinners only.
games.why: Jesus blessed bread on a hillside and at a plain supper; Paul gave thanks in a storm. the pause names food as a gift.

practice: If there's food or a drink near you, hold it a moment before tasting: notice its smell, its warmth, the hands it passed through to reach you.
If you pray, say a grace you already know, or a plain thank you; if not, let the first taste be slow and noticed. With nothing at hand, bring your last meal back to mind and taste it again in memory.

wordCard.voice: Grace at the table. A short pause to bless God and give thanks for food, as Jesus did over the loaves.

orig.note: Matthew's Greek for he blessed, as Jesus looked up over the loaves.

carryVoice: Your line: before every meal. Some bless at the start of the plate and some at the end, and both say thank you. See you at the next table.
